approved_text: Is it true that for every integer sequence a_0, a_1, … in which, for all sufficiently large n, a_{n+1} is the least integer exceeding a_n not of the form a_i + a_j (i, j ≤ n), the differences a_{m+1} − a_m are eventually periodic?
draft: Is the following true? For every integer sequence a_0, a_1, a_2, ... such that, for all sufficiently large n, a_{n+1} is the least integer greater than a_n that is not of the form a_i + a_j with i, j ≤ n, the differences a_{m+1} − a_m are eventually periodic with some period p > 0.
source_docstrings:
Let $A=\{a_1 < \cdots < a_k\}$ be a finite set of integers and extend it to an infinite
sequence $\overline{A}=\{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \}$ by defining $a_{n+1}$ for $n \geq k$ to be
the least integer exceeding $a_n$ which is not of the form $a_i + a_j$ with $i,j \leq n$.
Is it true that the sequence of differences $a_{m+1}-a_m$ is eventually periodic?

This problem is discussed under Problem 7 on Green's open problems list.
source_lean:
theorem erdos_341 :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∀ (a : ℕ → ℤ),
        (∀ᶠ n in atTop,
          IsLeast { x | a n < x ∧ x ∉ { a i + a j | (i ≤ n) (j ≤ n) } } (a (n + 1))) →
        let d := fun i ↦ a (i + 1) - a i
        ∃ p > 0, ∀ᶠ m in atTop, d (m + p) = d m
